stories.title: Previewing GPT-5.6: Sol, Terra, and Luna
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
OpenAI previewed GPT-5.6 as a three-model series: Sol (flagship), Terra (balanced, everyday use), and Luna (fast, low-cost). Terra matches GPT-5.5 performance at half the price; Luna targets the lowest-cost tier in the lineup.

↳ THE REAL STORY
This is OpenAI formalizing a tiered model strategy that Anthropic and Google have already normalized. For builders, Terra is the immediately interesting one: GPT-5.5-level output at 2x lower cost changes the math on high-volume workloads — summarization pipelines, classification, RAG retrieval layers — where you were previously paying flagship prices for tasks that don't need flagship reasoning. Luna positions as the new default for latency-sensitive applications where cost-per-token is the primary constraint. Sol's role is less clear from the excerpt alone, but "flagship" suggests it's the reasoning-heavy option for complex agentic tasks.
stories.considerations: The naming convention — Sol, Terra, Luna — is cosmetic, but the versioning (GPT-5.6) raises a real question: OpenAI is now shipping point releases faster than the ecosystem can benchmark them. Developers who built evals against GPT-5.5 will need to re-run them for Terra before trusting the "competitive performance" claim, since OpenAI's own comparisons are rarely apples-to-apples on domain-specific tasks. Also worth noting: "limited preview" means most teams can't act on this yet, and by the time broad access arrives, the competitive landscape may have shifted again.

stories.title: What happened after 2,000 people tried to hack my AI assistant
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Fernando Irarrázaval ran a public red-team challenge — hackmyclaw.com — inviting anyone to extract secrets from his OpenClaw AI assistant via email. Around 2,000 participants made roughly 6,000 attempts, costing him ~$500 in token spend.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The experiment is one of the more honest stress-tests of prompt injection defenses you'll find documented publicly. Rather than internal QA or synthetic adversarial prompts, it used real attackers with real motivation — which surfaces attack patterns that controlled testing misses. For developers shipping AI assistants that process inbound user content (emails, tickets, form submissions), the dataset of what actually worked versus what didn't is more useful than any benchmark.
stories.considerations: The excerpt cuts off before the result, which is the only number that matters here. If the secrets held, that's a meaningful data point for system-prompt hardening. If they didn't, it's a cautionary tale about trusting LLM-layer defenses for anything sensitive. Either way, the $500 cost for 6,000 adversarial inputs is a reminder that public red-team challenges have a real invoice attached — and that motivated attackers are patient enough to run high volumes when there's no rate limiting or cost friction on their end.

stories.title: What Should Be Done
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Hyperdimensional's latest piece argues the current frontier AI model release cycle creates a structurally broken market: labs spend enormous sums training models, recoup costs in a narrow post-release window, then watch those models become obsolete — leaving developers who built on them stranded.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The practical problem for builders is deprecation risk. If a significant share of a model's commercial value is extracted in the first few months post-release, labs have little financial incentive to maintain API stability or long support windows. Developers integrating a frontier model today are essentially betting on a short shelf life — which forces either constant re-evaluation and prompt re-engineering cycles, or accepting degraded performance as the model ages out. Neither is a good default for production systems.
stories.considerations: The excerpt cuts off before the argument lands, so it's hard to evaluate what 'should be done' actually proposes. That matters: diagnosing the deprecation treadmill is easy; the interesting question is whether the fix is contractual (longer support SLAs), economic (different pricing models), or structural (open weights as a hedge). Without seeing the prescription, this reads as a well-framed problem statement waiting for a solution that may or may not hold up.

stories.title: Quoting Timothy B. Lee
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Timothy B. Lee, via Simon Willison, pushes back on the claim that LLMs require no skill to use — comparing it to saying management has no learning curve because employees follow orders.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The analogy is sharper than it looks. A manager who gives vague, poorly-structured direction gets vague, poorly-structured output — and blames the employee. Same dynamic with LLMs. Prompt quality, context framing, knowing when to decompose a task, recognizing a hallucination versus a confident correct answer — none of that is obvious on day one. The "just type what you want" framing sets up developers and teams to underinvest in the actual skill of working with these models, then conclude the models don't work.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
The flip side of this argument is worth holding onto: if LLM use genuinely requires significant skill, that skill is currently invisible, untaught, and unevenly distributed. Companies are deploying AI tooling to employees with zero training and measuring adoption, not effectiveness. The learning curve exists — it's just that nobody's designed a curriculum for it yet, and most orgs won't until the output quality gap becomes impossible to ignore.

stories.title: Incident Report: CVE-2026-LGTM
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Andrew Nesbitt published a fictional incident report — CVE-2026-LGTM — depicting a supply chain compromise that propagates silently through AI-assisted code review. The scenario: two competing AI review agents, both attached to the same downstream pull request, enter a disagreement loop while reviewing a dependency bump for `foxhole-lz4`.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The story is a thought experiment, but the failure mode it describes is real and already partially observable. When AI reviewers auto-approve PRs — or worse, argue with each other while humans disengage — the social contract of code review collapses. The 'LGTM' becomes a rubber stamp issued by a model that has no skin in the game. In practice, teams using AI review tools today are already seeing reduced human attention on dependency bumps, exactly the class of change most exploited in supply chain attacks (see: XZ Utils, event-stream). The fictional CVE name is the punchline, but the mechanism — AI agents providing cover for malicious commits — is a plausible near-term threat vector, not science fiction.
stories.considerations: The non-obvious implication here is about liability diffusion. When two AI agents disagree and a human merges anyway — or when one agent approves and no human reads it — who owns the incident? Current AI review tooling has no audit trail designed for post-breach forensics. The catch with AI code review isn't that it's wrong more often than humans; it's that it's wrong in ways that are harder to attribute, easier to exploit deliberately, and almost impossible to catch in a standard retrospective. Worth asking your team: if an AI reviewer approved a malicious commit last week, would you know?
